newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOTM aims to cut risk assets by 1-3 trillion yen.
newsitem.headline: BOTM aims to cut risk assets by 1-3 trillion yen.

text.p: Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd plans to cut its risk-weighted assets by one to three trillion yen as part of an effort to raise its BIS capital adequacy ratio, an official at the bank said on Wednesday.

The bank has a goal of raising its Tier One BIS ratio to above six percent from the current 4.97 percent, and its return on equity (ROE) to above eight percent from 1.5 percent over the next three years, the official said.

"To achieve this goal, we would need to reduce our risk-weighted assets. It is difficult to set a precise target because there are a number of variable factors such as movements in foreign exchange rates and growth in loans," the official said.
"However, judging from the current size of our capital, we may need to cut risk-weighted assets by one to three trillion yen," he added.

Under the capital adequacy rules set by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), banks operating internationally are required to set aside capital equal to eight percent of assets judged to be at risk.
At least half of the eight percent of capital required to be set against the risk-weighted assets must be Tier One capital, which comprises equity and disclosed reserves.
As an effort to cut back on risk-weighted assets, Tokyo-Mitsubishi last week securitised 105 billion yen worth of loans it made to Japanese companies.

Under the deal, Wizard Finance, a special purpose company set up by Tokyo-Mitsubishi in the Cayman Islands, issued 95 billion yen worth of euroyen and eurodollar bonds and 10 billion yen worth of subordinated euroyen bonds with these loans as collateral.
The securitisation deal, the biggest done by any Japanese bank in the eurobond market, allows Tokyo-Mitsubishi to fully remove 105 billion yen worth of loan assets from its balance sheet.

"As in the United States, the market for asset-backed securities is likely to gradually develop in Japan. We would like to consider issuing more of them in the future," said the official, but added the bank had not set a specific figure for the value of future issues.
